title: How they say it there
job: Regional and generational speech; what marks an outsider
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: al-fuṣḥā is Modern Standard Arabic, al-ʿāmmiyya is the everyday speech of a place, and a lahja is one region's version of it. Those three words are the whole map, and this module is where the course buys them.

The nisba is the -ī the ladder has been using since L1-M1's al-Hind, named here as a rule: add it to a place or a noun and you get an adjective. ash-shām → shāmī, miṣr → miṣrī, balad → baladī, shaʿb → shaʿbī. The feminine is -iyya.

ENGLISH MAPS DIALECT ONTO ACCENT — same language, different sounds. Arabic's varieties differ in grammar and in core vocabulary, and al-fuṣḥā is nobody's mother tongue, so there is no neutral spoken Arabic to fall back on the way there is a neutral English.

FORMAL IS NOT THE SAFE DEFAULT. An English speaker assumes the formal register works anywhere; in the street al-fuṣḥā marks an outsider as reliably as the wrong dialect does. It is a passport rather than a disguise: it gets you through everywhere and it never makes you a local.

Every line this course writes is al-fuṣḥā (#198), and this module does not break that. The dialect forms it is ABOUT are named and described, never spoken: you learn to say that a word is Levantine without having to produce the Levantine word.
yaqūlūn and yatakallamūn are L3-M5's yaqūl and L1-M10's yatakallam wearing the masculine plural -ūn. A new shape of a verb you already own, not a new tense.

The generational observation has one shape: jīl al-kibār or ash-shabāb, then the plural verb. It reports what a group says and never claims the speaker says it — which is what makes it safe to use about people in the room.
yaʿnī introduces the gloss of what was just said — that is, in other words. ʿumūman (generally) is the hedge that keeps an observation about a whole country from sounding like a law.

sentences.display: al-fuṣḥā lugha wāḥida, wa al-lahajāt kathīra
sentences.cue: Standard Arabic is one language, and the dialects are many.
sentences.literal: the-standard language one, and the-dialects many

words.note: Literally the most eloquent. It is what this course teaches, what the news is read in, and what nobody speaks at home.
A lahja is one region's spoken Arabic. Naming it is not judging it: a lahja is not a mistake, and saying so is half of this module.
Many. L1-M1 bought kathīran, the adverb a lot; this is the adjective underneath it, and it agrees: kathīra with a feminine noun, kathīr with a masculine one.

sentences.trap: One language with many dialects sounds like English and its accents. It is not the same claim: the varieties differ in grammar and in everyday words, and no one of them is the neutral one.
sentences.sound: al-FUṢ-ḥā: the ṣ is the heavy s made with the tongue flat, and the ḥ is the breathy h from the throat. la-ha-JĀT ends long.

variations.cue: The dialects are many, and Standard Arabic is one.
variations.changed: the order — the plurality first, when that is the point being made

variations.cue: Standard Arabic is not a dialect.
variations.changed: the claim — what al-fuṣḥā is not, which is the commoner thing to have to say

mistake.why: lugha is feminine, so the number agrees: wāḥida. L1-M8 bought both forms; this is the sentence that makes you choose one.

sentences.usage: The opening move of any conversation about Arabic with someone who has just asked which Arabic you are learning.

sentences.display: fī ash-shām yaqūlūn kalima wa fī al-maghrib yaqūlūn ukhrā
sentences.script: في الشام يقولون كلمة وفي المغرب يقولون أخرى
sentences.cue: In the Levant they say one word and in the Maghreb they say another.
sentences.literal: in the-Levant they-say word and in the-Maghreb they-say another

words.cue: the Levant — Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine
words.note: One name for the whole eastern Mediterranean region. The sun letter sh swallows the l of al-, which L1-M2 already showed you.
L3-M5's yaqūl in the masculine plural: -ūn on the end. The impersonal they of an observation, with nobody named.

words.cue: the Maghreb — Morocco and the west
words.note: The place where the sun sets, hence the west. It names both Morocco and the wider region, and context decides which.

sentences.trap: English says they say it differently there and stops. Arabic wants the region named: fī ash-shām, fī al-maghrib. A bare there is not enough to be understood as a claim about a variety.
sentences.sound: fī ash-SHĀM: one long ā. al-MAGH-rib opens with the gh, the sound of a French r made at the back of the throat.

variations.cue: In the Gulf they say a different word.
variations.changed: the region — the Gulf, and one half of the claim instead of two

variations.cue: In Egypt they say a different word.
variations.changed: the region — Egypt, whose speech a learner meets first on screen

mistake.why: yaqūl is he says — one named man. The observation is about a region, so the verb goes plural: yaqūlūn. The singular quietly turns a fact about a country into gossip about a person.

sentences.usage: Explaining to a friend why the word they just heard is not the word you taught them.
sentences.mnemonic: -ūn is the crowd on the end of the verb.

sentences.display: hādhihi al-kalima shāmiyya, wa laysat fuṣḥā
sentences.cue: This word is Levantine, and it is not Standard Arabic.
sentences.literal: this the-word Levantine, and not standard

words.note: A single word, as against kalām, which is speech in general. The plural is kalimāt.
The nisba: a place name plus -ī, feminine -iyya. It agrees with the noun, so a kalima is shāmiyya and a shakhṣ is shāmī.

sentences.trap: English has no productive way to do this — Levantine, Egyptian and Moroccan are separate words a learner has to know. Arabic builds them all from the place name with one ending, so the whole set is free once the rule is.
sentences.sound: shā-MIY-ya: the double y is held, and it is what separates the feminine shāmiyya from the masculine shāmī.

variations.display: hādhihi al-kalima miṣriyya, wa laysat fuṣḥā
variations.cue: This word is Egyptian, and it is not Standard Arabic.
variations.changed: the region — the same frame with a different nisba dropped into it

variations.cue: This word is Standard Arabic.
variations.changed: the verdict — the word turns out to be standard after all

mistake.why: kalima is feminine, so the nisba is too: shāmiyya. The masculine shāmī belongs to a man from the Levant, not to a word.

sentences.usage: When somebody asks what a word you both just heard was, and the honest answer is where it is from.
sentences.mnemonic: Place plus -ī, and -iyya when the thing it describes is feminine.

sentences.display: al-ʿāmmiyya ṣaʿba ʿalā al-ajnabī fī al-khalīj wa fī al-maghrib
sentences.script: العامية صعبة على الأجنبي في الخليج وفي المغرب
sentences.cue: The colloquial is hard for a foreigner in the Gulf and in the Maghreb.
sentences.literal: the-colloquial hard on the-foreigner in the-Gulf and in the-Maghreb

words.note: From ʿāmm, general or common: the speech of everybody. It is the opposite pole from al-fuṣḥā, and it is never written in this course.
A foreigner, neutrally — it describes where you are from, not how welcome you are. It is itself a nisba, on ajnab.
The Gulf, and by extension the countries on it. The kh is the sound at the end of Scottish loch.

sentences.trap: A learner hears this and reaches for al-fuṣḥā as the safe fallback. It is safe for being understood and unsafe for sounding like anyone: formal Arabic in a Gulf café is correct and audibly foreign.
sentences.sound: al-ʿĀM-miy-ya opens on the ʿayn, a squeeze low in the throat, not the hamza's clean catch. ṢAʿ-ba has both: heavy ṣ, then ʿayn.

variations.display: al-ʿāmmiyya ṣaʿba ʿalā al-ajnabī fī ash-shām
variations.script: العامية صعبة على الأجنبي في الشام
variations.cue: The colloquial is hard for a foreigner in the Levant.
variations.changed: one region instead of two — the ordinary length of the remark

variations.cue: Standard Arabic is easy for a foreigner.
variations.changed: the other half of the claim — what is easy, and why a learner starts here

mistake.why: al-ʿāmmiyya is feminine — the -iyya ending says so — so the predicate is ṣaʿba. L1-M9 bought both; the agreement is the choice.

sentences.usage: Answering the question every learner is asked: why are you studying the one Arabic nobody speaks?
sentences.mnemonic: ʿāmm is common; al-ʿāmmiyya is the common tongue.

sentences.cue: The older generation says old words.

words.note: A generation of people. jīl al-kibār and jīl ash-shabāb are the two the module needs, and they are a possessive pair: generation of the elders.
The plural of L1-M3's kabīr used as a noun: the big ones, meaning the old. It is respectful, not a complaint.

sentences.trap: English attaches age to slang and expects the young to have the odd words. Here it runs both ways: the elders keep words the young have dropped, and the observation is neutral about which is better.
sentences.sound: JĪL is one long syllable. al-ki-BĀR takes the stress on the long ā at the end.

variations.cue: The younger generation says different words.
variations.changed: the generation — the young, in the same frame

variations.cue: Older people say old words.
variations.changed: the subject — the people themselves, so the verb goes plural

mistake.why: The subject is jīl, one generation, so the verb is singular: yaqūl. The plural verb belongs with al-kibār as the subject, which is the second variation.

sentences.usage: Explaining a word your host's grandmother used that nobody under forty has said in years.
sentences.mnemonic: jīl is one thing, however many people are in it.

sentences.cue: Young people speak in a different style.

words.note: A collective: the young as a body, not a countable group. It takes a plural verb even though the noun looks singular.
L1-M10's yatakallam with the masculine plural -ūn, the same ending yaqūlūn takes. One rule, both verbs.
How something is said rather than what is said. bi-uslūb is in a style — L1-M2's bi- doing its ordinary work.
Different, in the sense of not the same as. Feminine mukhtalifa. It is descriptive and carries no verdict.

sentences.trap: Different style in English hints that something is wrong with it. mukhtalif does not: it is the flat observation, and the disapproval an English speaker hears in it has to be added deliberately if you want it.
sentences.sound: ya-ta-kal-la-MŪN: five syllables, stress on the long ū at the end. us-LŪB begins with a hamza, a small catch before the u.

variations.cue: Older people speak in an old-fashioned style.
variations.changed: the generation — the elders, and the style that goes with them

variations.cue: She speaks in a different style.
variations.changed: one named speaker instead of a whole generation, so the verb goes singular

mistake.why: ash-shabāb is a collective and takes the plural verb yatakallamūn. The singular reads as one young man, which is not the observation you were making.

sentences.usage: Said about a group of teenagers on the next table, without any suggestion that they are speaking badly.
sentences.mnemonic: uslūb is the how; kalām is the what.

sentences.display: hādhā kalām shaʿbī, wa laysa fuṣḥā
sentences.cue: This is popular speech, and it is not Standard Arabic.
sentences.literal: this speech popular, and not standard

words.note: Speech in general, uncountable — from the same root as yatakallam. One item of it is a kalima.
The nisba again, on a noun rather than a place: shaʿb, a people, gives shaʿbī. baladī, from balad, is its close cousin — local, homegrown.

sentences.trap: Popular and folk sound faintly patronising in English. shaʿbī and baladī are warm words for food, music and phrases that belong to a place, and using them as an insult is a transfer error.
sentences.sound: ka-LĀM has the long ā in the middle. shaʿ-BĪ puts the ʿayn right after the sh, then the long ī of the nisba.

variations.display: hādhā kalām baladī, wa laysa fuṣḥā
variations.cue: This is local speech, and it is not Standard Arabic.
variations.changed: the nisba — baladī, the homegrown one, in place of shaʿbī

variations.display: hādhā kalām shaʿbī, wa laysa gharīb
variations.cue: This is popular speech, and it is not strange.
variations.changed: the second half — popular is not the same as odd, which is the correction worth making

mistake.why: kalām is masculine, so the nisba is shaʿbī. The feminine shaʿbiyya waits for a feminine noun — kalima shaʿbiyya, lahja shaʿbiyya.

sentences.usage: Placing a phrase for somebody who asked whether they can use it in an exam. The answer is where it lives, not whether it is allowed.
sentences.mnemonic: shaʿb is a people; shaʿbī is theirs.

sentences.display: fī kull balad nabra mukhtalifa, wa hādhā ʿādī
sentences.script: في كل بلد نبرة مختلفة، وهذا عادي
sentences.cue: In every country there is a different intonation, and that is normal.
sentences.literal: in every country intonation different, and this normal

words.note: A country, or the town you are from — the scale is set by context. It is the noun baladī is built on.
The melody of a sentence — the part of an accent that survives even when somebody switches to al-fuṣḥā.

sentences.trap: An English speaker's accent model gets this one claim right — and intonation is exactly the part that is NOT what makes the varieties different. The tune is the surface; the grammar underneath moves too.
sentences.sound: NAB-ra is short and clipped, the b closing the first syllable. mukh-TA-li-fa opens on the kh of Scottish loch.

variations.cue: In the Levant there is a different intonation.
variations.changed: a named region instead of every country, which makes it an observation rather than a rule

variations.cue: In every country there is a different dialect.
variations.changed: the claim moves up from the tune to the whole variety

mistake.why: nabra is feminine — the -a on the end says so — so its adjective is mukhtalifa. mukhtalif waits for a masculine noun.

sentences.usage: Said while somebody is telling you they cannot hear any difference between two speakers.
sentences.mnemonic: nabra is the tune the words are carried on.

sentences.display: huwa yatakallam al-fuṣḥā ʿumūman, wa hādhā ʿādī
sentences.script: هو يتكلم الفصحى عمومًا، وهذا عادي
sentences.cue: He generally speaks Standard Arabic, and that is normal.
sentences.literal: he speaks the-standard generally, and this normal

words.note: Generally. It is the hedge that keeps a remark about a person or a country from being heard as a law about them.
Ordinary, unremarkable. Saying a usage is ʿādī is the kindest verdict this module can hand down: not wrong, not odd, just usual.

sentences.trap: That is normal in English can sound dismissive. ʿādī is the opposite — it is reassurance, the word you use to tell somebody their Arabic did not sound strange.
sentences.sound: ʿu-MŪ-man: the ʿayn first, then a long ū, then the -an ending that L1 taught on adverbs. ʿĀ-dī opens on the ʿayn too.

variations.cue: I generally speak Standard Arabic.
variations.changed: the speaker — first person, which is the honest sentence for a learner

variations.cue: He generally speaks the colloquial.
variations.changed: the variety — the colloquial, which this course names and never writes

mistake.why: dāʾiman is always, and about a living person it is almost never true. ʿumūman leaves room for the kitchen and the taxi, which is where the fuṣḥā stops.

sentences.usage: Describing a colleague whose Arabic a visitor found unexpectedly easy to follow.
sentences.mnemonic: ʿumūman is the word that stops a remark becoming a rule.

sentences.display: hādhā ash-shakhṣ yaqūl kalima shāmiyya, yaʿnī huwa min ash-shām
sentences.script: هذا الشخص يقول كلمة شامية، يعني هو من الشام
sentences.cue: This person says a Levantine word — meaning, he is from the Levant.
sentences.literal: this the-person says word Levantine, that-is he from the-Levant

words.note: A person, of either sex, when you do not want to say man or woman. Another sun-letter article: ash-, not al-.
Literally it means. It introduces the gloss of what you just said, and it is the commonest word in spoken Arabic that this course can write.

sentences.trap: English would put the inference first — he must be Levantine, because he said X. Arabic runs the other way: the evidence, then yaʿnī, then the conclusion. Reversing it is understood but sounds argued rather than observed.
sentences.sound: ash-SHAKHṢ ends on a cluster of kh and heavy ṣ with no vowel between them. YAʿ-nī has the ʿayn closing the first syllable.

variations.cue: This person says a Maghrebi word.
variations.changed: the nisba, and the inference left unsaid

variations.display: hādhihi al-kalima shāmiyya, yaʿnī hiya min ash-shām
variations.script: هذه الكلمة شامية، يعني هي من الشام
variations.cue: This word is Levantine — meaning, it is from the Levant.
variations.changed: the subject — the word rather than the speaker, which is the safer thing to say aloud

mistake.display: hādhā ash-shakhṣ shāmī, yaʿnī huwa yaqūl kalima shāmiyya
mistake.script: هذا الشخص شامي، يعني هو يقول كلمة شامية
mistake.why: The halves are swapped. yaʿnī goes from evidence to conclusion, never from conclusion back to evidence; reversed, it reads as an accusation being justified.

sentences.usage: Working out where somebody is from, quietly, from one word they used.
sentences.mnemonic: Evidence, yaʿnī, conclusion — in that order.

comprehensionPool.display: al-fuṣḥā lugha wāḥida, wa al-lahajāt kathīra
comprehensionPool.cue: Standard Arabic is one language, and the dialects are many.
In the Maghreb they say a different word.
The older generation says old words.
Young people speak in a different style.
The colloquial is hard for a foreigner.

comprehensionPool.display: hādhā kalām shaʿbī, wa laysa fuṣḥā
comprehensionPool.cue: This is popular speech, and it is not Standard Arabic.
In every country there is a different intonation.
This person is from the Levant.
